title: Designing a demo request that respects time
metaTitle: A demo request that respects time
excerpt: Ask only what you need to prepare, and say what the demo will cover. A long form spends the interest the page just earned.
alt: Three pale speckled bottles on a gray surface, two holding dried seed heads, a small still life for an article about asking only what a demo needs.
caption: A few objects, enough to know what you are looking at. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How many fields should a demo request have?
faqs.answer: Keep the fields you will actually use to prepare: a name, an email, and the job they want to see, plus a URL if you need to look before the call. Company size, budget, and a survey of how they found you can wait until you are talking. A required field you never mention in the meeting is a toll, not a qualification.

faqs.question: What should the page say about the meeting itself?
faqs.answer: Say how long it is, what you will look at, and what you will not do in that time. Name the kind of person who will be there. A buyer is trading a half hour, and an agenda makes that trade legible. A label that only says hello does not.

faqs.question: Where should an error appear?
faqs.answer: Put the error in text next to the field, and keep what the person already typed. A red border alone is not an explanation, and a cleared form makes people leave. Move focus to the first problem so they can fix it and send the note again.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Demo request ux is the design of a small door. Ask only what the team needs in order to prepare, and tell the buyer what the demo will cover. A twelve-field form is a tax on interest the page has already earned.

The form sits between a promise and a conversation. It should sound like the page that sent the person here, and it should leave them sure what the next half hour is for.

## What you need in order to prepare

Write down the facts that change how you spend the demo. Usually that is a short list. Their name. A way to reach them. The URL of the product or the site they have now. The job they want to see. Anything else can be asked out loud, where a confused answer can be followed with a question.

If you sell to companies, you may need the company name so you do not walk in blind. You rarely need headcount, budget, a dropdown of industries, and a paragraph on their stack before you have agreed the meeting is real. Those fields feel like diligence. They read like a toll.

Preparation is concrete. "I need the URL so I can open it before we talk." That is a reason a buyer accepts. "Help us route you to the right specialist" is a reason they invent, and many of them will invent an exit instead. If you are a small team, say so. One person will read the note and show up. The form should not pretend there is a routing department.

Put the reason next to the field, in one clause. [The W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) groups this under content people can understand: labels and instructions that say what is being asked. A floating placeholder is not a label. When the field is filled, the placeholder disappears, and the buyer can no longer see what they were meant to type. Keep the label visible.

## Tell them what the demo will cover

The form is also a promise about the meeting. Before the fields, write three lines. How long it is. What you will look at. What you will not do. A thirty-minute look at their current signup, with a recommendation on what to change first, is a demo a founder can accept. A "quick intro to the platform" is a fog, and fogs attract people who wanted something else.

Match the promise to the page they came from. If they clicked from a page about onboarding, the demo should be about onboarding. If they came from a migration story, do not greet them with a generic tour. The seam between the article and the form is where interest goes to die. Same words, same job, same next step.

Say who will be on the call. A founder, a designer who will also build, a solutions person. Buyers are deciding whether to give away a half hour of their calendar. The name of the shape of the meeting helps more than a stock photo of a headset. If the meeting is a fit check and not a custom build, say that too. Limits make the yes easier.

[Nielsen Norman Group's research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) on visits is a fair clock for this screen. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and a clear value proposition has to land inside about 10 seconds if you want the rest of their time. The value on this page is the meeting, described. Spend the opening on that description, not on a second headline about how excited you are to connect.

## Fields that tax the interest

Count the fields. Then remove any field whose answer you will not read before the call. A dropdown of company size that nobody mentions in the meeting is decoration with a cost. A required phone number, for a conversation that will happen on a video link, is a cost. A "how did you hear about us" survey is a cost you can pay later, on the call, in one sentence.

Group what remains by the decision, not by the database. Who you are. What you want to see. How to send the invite. Three groups, with a short heading each, feel like a conversation. One long column of twenty inputs feels like paperwork from a vendor who has not looked at the product.

Make the optional fields look optional, and mean it. If you mark a field optional and then the sales note complains when it is empty, the form is lying. Required should mean "we cannot prepare without this." Everything else waits.

Watch the mobile screen. A form that is reasonable on a wide monitor becomes a tunnel on a phone, which is where a lot of demo intent actually starts. One column. Large enough type. The button visible after the last field, not stranded under a legal essay. If the legal note is required, keep it short and adjacent to the action, in readable type.

## Labels, errors, and the order of questions

Order the questions the way a person would answer them out loud. Name, work email, the thing they want to see, the link. Asking for a budget before they have said what the demo is about feels like the meeting already went sour. You can talk about money when you both know the shape of the work.

When something is wrong, say so next to the field, in text. Color alone is not an explanation. "Enter a work email so we can send the invite" is an error a person can fix. A red border and a toast at the top of the page is a puzzle. [WCAG's guidance on understandable forms](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the reference for identifying the error in text and giving a label that stays put. You do not need a certification project to follow that much.

Do not clear the form when validation fails. Nothing makes a buyer close a tab faster than retyping a paragraph because one field was fussy. Keep their words. Move focus to the first problem. Let them fix it and send again.

Autocomplete helps more than a clever layout. Name, email, and organization are standard fields browsers already know. Use those meanings so a phone can fill them. A custom widget that looks like a text field and is not one will fight the browser, and the browser was trying to save the buyer time. That is the whole point of this page.

## The page around the form

The form should not be the only thing on the page. A buyer who is still deciding needs a reminder of the product and of what the meeting covers, beside the fields or just above them. One screenshot, one sentence, the three lines about the agenda. Then the form. A page that is only inputs assumes the decision is finished. Often it is not.

If you have a calendar embed, use it after the minimum facts, or beside them, not as a substitute for saying what the meeting is. An empty calendar with no agenda is a polite way to ask someone to gamble a slot. Show the next three available times if you can. A wall of a whole month is a second task.

Keep the visual language of the site. If the marketing page is quiet and the form is a bright template from another tool, the buyer feels a handoff to a different company. Same type, same button, same tone. The form is a page you publish, not a widget you tolerate.

On a product like the public interfaces in Got Next or Leadly, the request to see a demo should feel like the product, not like a separate marketing skin. If your app is dense because the work is dense, the form can still be short. Density in the product is not an excuse for density in the request.

## What happens after they send it

The thank-you state is part of the design. Say that the note arrived. Say when they will hear back, in a range you actually keep. Say whether a calendar link is coming by email or whether they just booked the time. A blank success message, or a redirect to the homepage, makes people submit twice and then write to ask if it worked.

Send an email that repeats the agenda in the same voice. One next action. Add the invite to the calendar. If you need more information, ask one question, not a second form with the twelve fields you were wise enough to cut. The email is a continuation of the page. A sequence of five tips is a different product, and they did not sign up for a course.

Inside the team, decide who reads the note and how fast. A form that promises a reply and then sits in a shared inbox until Thursday has a design problem even if the fields were perfect. Write the owner's name down. If that person is out, name the backup. The buyer cannot see your inbox. They can feel the silence.

Use the submissions as a critique of the form. If people constantly write "not sure this is relevant" in the open field, your agenda line is vague. If they skip a field you marked required and your tool allows it, your required set is fictional. Adjust the form quarterly, not every time one record looks odd.

## The limit of screening

A short form will let a few unqualified people book. That is an acceptable cost. The alternative, a gate that only a determined buyer will finish, screens out the careful people you wanted and keeps the ones who will type anything. You can decline a meeting in a sentence. You cannot recover a founder who left at field eight.

Do not use the form to do strategy. It will not tell you your positioning. It will not replace a conversation about scope. If you notice that every demo starts with the same confusion, fix the page that sent them, not the form. Adding a field called "what are you hoping to achieve" is how teams collect essays they do not read.

If your real next step is a self-serve trial, do not disguise it as a demo request. Let them start. Offer a human for the people who want one. Two doors, labeled, are kinder than one door that pretends to be both.

Once someone is in the product, they still need proof that it moves. A public note of what changed, written in their language, is the subject of [a changelog the public can read](/blog/a-changelog-the-public-can-read). Read that next if your demo keeps promising momentum you never show after signup.

If you want to see how a product surface can stay specific from the first screen through the interface, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The useful comparison is whether a stranger can tell what the meeting, or the product, is for before they are asked to type.
